claim: HSF1 deficiency may decrease ERα level in ER-positive breast cancer cells.
source: We found that an HSF1 deficiency may decrease ERα level, attenuate the mitogenic action of E2, counteract E2-stimulated cell scattering, and reduce adhesion to collagens and cell motility in ER-positive breast cancer cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from western blot analyses showing reduced ERα levels in HSF1-deficient cells (Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).

claim: HSF1 deficiency may attenuate the mitogenic action of E2 in ER-positive breast cancer cells.
source: We found that an HSF1 deficiency may decrease ERα level, attenuate the mitogenic action of E2, counteract E2-stimulated cell scattering, and reduce adhesion to collagens and cell motility in ER-positive breast cancer cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing weaker E2-stimulated proliferation in HSF1-deficient cells (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).

claim: HSF1 deficiency may counteract E2-stimulated cell scattering in ER-positive breast cancer cells.
source: We found that an HSF1 deficiency may decrease ERα level, attenuate the mitogenic action of E2, counteract E2-stimulated cell scattering, and reduce adhesion to collagens and cell motility in ER-positive breast cancer cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from F-actin staining showing reduced cell scattering in HSF1-deficient cells after E2 treatment (Figure 1E and F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1I).

claim: HSF1 deficiency may reduce adhesion to collagens in ER-positive breast cancer cells.
source: We found that an HSF1 deficiency may decrease ERα level, attenuate the mitogenic action of E2, counteract E2-stimulated cell scattering, and reduce adhesion to collagens and cell motility in ER-positive breast cancer cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from cell adhesion assays showing reduced adhesion to collagens I and IV in HSF1-deficient cells (Figure 1G).

claim: HSF1 deficiency may reduce cell motility in ER-positive breast cancer cells.
source: We found that an HSF1 deficiency may decrease ERα level, attenuate the mitogenic action of E2, counteract E2-stimulated cell scattering, and reduce adhesion to collagens and cell motility in ER-positive breast cancer cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Boyden chamber assays showing reduced migration in HSF1-deficient cells (Figure 1H, Figure 1—figure supplement 1H).

claim: The stimulatory effect of E2 on the transcriptome is largely weaker in HSF1-deficient cells.
source: The stimulatory effect of E2 on the transcriptome is largely weaker in HSF1-deficient cells, in part due to the higher basal expression of E2-dependent genes, which correlates with the enhanced binding of unliganded ERα to chromatin in such cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data showing that approximately 20% of genes responding to E2 in HSF1+ cells did not respond similarly in HSF1− cells, and that many genes responded less effectively in HSF1− cells (Figure 2A).

claim: HSF1-deficient cells show higher basal expression of E2-dependent genes.
source: The stimulatory effect of E2 on the transcriptome is largely weaker in HSF1-deficient cells, in part due to the higher basal expression of E2-dependent genes, which correlates with the enhanced binding of unliganded ERα to chromatin in such cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq and RT-qPCR data showing higher basal expression of several E2-dependent genes in untreated HSF1-deficient cells (Figure 2C, Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1G).

claim: HSF1-deficient cells show enhanced binding of unliganded ERα to chromatin.
source: The stimulatory effect of E2 on the transcriptome is largely weaker in HSF1-deficient cells, in part due to the higher basal expression of E2-dependent genes, which correlates with the enhanced binding of unliganded ERα to chromatin in such cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq data showing more ERα binding sites and increased number of tags per peak in unstimulated HSF1-deficient cells compared to HSF1-proficient cells (Figure 3A and B).

claim: HSF1 and ERα can cooperate directly in E2-stimulated regulation of transcription.
source: HSF1 and ERα can cooperate directly in E2-stimulated regulation of transcription, and HSF1 potentiates the action of ERα through a mechanism involving chromatin reorganization.
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq data showing overlapping binding sites for HSF1 and ERα after E2 treatment (Figure 4B, Figure 5), and by 3C data showing HSF1-dependent chromatin interactions (Figure 4E).

claim: HSF1 potentiates the action of ERα through a mechanism involving chromatin reorganization.
source: HSF1 and ERα can cooperate directly in E2-stimulated regulation of transcription, and HSF1 potentiates the action of ERα through a mechanism involving chromatin reorganization.
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq data combined with ChIA-PET data showing that HSF1-binding sites map to ERα anchor regions (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1), and by 3C data showing HSF1-dependent chromatin loop formation (Figure 4E).

claim: HSF1 deficiency may increase the sensitivity to hormonal therapy (4-hydroxytamoxifen) in ER-positive breast cancer cells.
source: Furthermore, HSF1 deficiency may increase the sensitivity to hormonal therapy (4-hydroxytamoxifen) or CDK4/6 inhibitors (palbociclib).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that 4-OHT treatment did not result in increased proliferation in HSF1-deficient cells, unlike in HSF1-proficient cells (Figure 8A).

claim: HSF1 deficiency may increase the sensitivity to CDK4/6 inhibitors (palbociclib) in ER-positive breast cancer cells.
source: Furthermore, HSF1 deficiency may increase the sensitivity to hormonal therapy (4-hydroxytamoxifen) or CDK4/6 inhibitors (palbociclib).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that the IC50 of palbociclib was more than twofold lower in HSF1− MCF7 cells than in HSF1+ cells (Figure 8C).

claim: HSF1 increases the transcriptome disparity in ER-positive breast cancer.
source: Analyses of data from The Cancer Genome Atlas database indicate that HSF1 increases the transcriptome disparity in ER-positive breast cancer and can enhance the genomic action of ERα.
evidence: This claim is supported by analyses of TCGA data showing that differences between ER+ and ER− cases were higher in the presence of high levels of HSF1 (Figure 7A, Figure 7C).

claim: HSF1 can enhance the genomic action of ERα in breast cancer.
source: Analyses of data from The Cancer Genome Atlas database indicate that HSF1 increases the transcriptome disparity in ER-positive breast cancer and can enhance the genomic action of ERα.
evidence: This claim is supported by analyses of TCGA data showing that the number of genes differentiating ER+ and ER− cases was higher in HSF1high cancers (Figure 7C), and that gene set enrichment analysis identified terms related to estrogen response as differentiating between ER+ and ER− cancers with different HSF1 levels (Figure 7D).

claim: Only in ER-positive cancers an elevated HSF1 level is associated with metastatic disease.
source: Moreover, only in ER-positive cancers an elevated HSF1 level is associated with metastatic disease.
evidence: This claim is supported by analyses of TCGA data showing that HSF1 expression level was higher in metastatic cases than in nonmetastatic ones only in the ER+ group (Figure 6F), and that metastatic tumors were overrepresented in ER+/HSF1high cases (Figure 6G, Figure 6H).

claim: Luminal adenocarcinomas constitute about 70% of all breast cancer cases.
source: Among them, luminal adenocarcinomas, characterized by the expression of estrogen receptors, constitute about 70% of all breast cancer cases.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about breast cancer classification and prevalence.

claim: ERα expression is most common in breast cancer.
source: ERα expression is most common in breast cancer, and its evaluation is the basis for determining the ER status.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about estrogen receptor expression in breast cancer.

claim: Estrogens are synthesized from cholesterol via androgens in the reaction catalyzed by aromatase.
source: The activity of estrogen receptors is modulated by steroid hormones, mainly estrogens, which are synthesized from cholesterol via androgens in the reaction catalyzed by aromatase (Fuentes and Silveyra, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Fuentes and Silveyra, 2019.

claim: Estrogens alongside mutations in BRCA1, BRCA2, CHEK2, TP53, STK11 (LKB1), PIK3CA, PTEN, and other genes are key etiological factors of breast cancer development.
source: According to epidemiological and experimental data, estrogens alongside the mutations in BRCA1 and BRCA2, CHEK2, TP53, STK11 (LKB1), PIK3CA, PTEN, and other genes, are key etiological factors of breast cancer development (Yaşar et al., 2017; Verigos and Magklara, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Yaşar et al., 2017 and Verigos and Magklara, 2015.

claim: Hormonal therapies targeting either estrogen production or the hormone receptor itself are widely used to block the mitogenic action of estrogens in patients with ER-positive breast cancer.
source: Nevertheless, hormonal therapies targeting either estrogen production (i.e., aromatase inhibitors) or the hormone receptor itself such as selective ER modulators (SERMs; i.e., tamoxifen) and selective ER degraders (SERDs; i.e., fulvestrant) are widely used to block the mitogenic action of estrogens in patients with ER-positive breast cancer (Renoir, 2012; Farcas et al., 2021), contributing to the decline in mortality from breast cancer in recent decades (Iwase et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Renoir, 2012; Farcas et al., 2021; and Iwase et al., 2021.

claim: 17β-estradiol (E2) stimulates activation of heat shock factor 1 (HSF1) in estrogen-dependent breast cancer cells via MAPK signaling.
source: Previously, we have found that the major female sex hormone 17β-estradiol (E2) stimulates activation of heat shock factor 1 (HSF1) in estrogen-dependent breast cancer cells via MAPK signaling (Vydra et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Vydra et al., 2019, which is the authors' previous work.

claim: HSF1 mainly regulates the expression of heat shock proteins (HSPs), which function as molecular chaperones and regulate protein homeostasis.
source: It mainly regulates the expression of the heat shock proteins (HSPs), which function as molecular chaperones and regulate protein homeostasis (Ran et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ran et al., 2007.

claim: HSF1-regulated chaperones control the activity of estrogen receptors.
source: HSF1-regulated chaperones control, among others, the activity of estrogen receptors (Echeverria and Picard, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Echeverria and Picard, 2010.

claim: ERs remain in an inactive state trapped in multimolecular chaperone complexes organized around HSP90, containing p23 (PTGES3), and immunophilins (FKBP4 or FKPB5).
source: ERs remain in an inactive state trapped in multimolecular chaperone complexes organized around HSP90, containing p23 (PTGES3), and immunophilins (FKBP4 or FKPB5) (Segnitz and Gehring, 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Segnitz and Gehring, 1995.

claim: Upon binding to E2, ERs dissociate from the chaperone complexes and become competent to dimerize and regulate the transcription.
source: Upon binding to E2, ERs dissociate from the chaperone complexes and become competent to dimerize and regulate the transcription.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about estrogen receptor activation.

claim: HSP90 is essential for ERα hormone binding.
source: HSP90 is essential for ERα hormone binding (Fliss et al., 2000), dimer formation (Powell et al., 2010), and binding to the EREs (Inano et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Fliss et al., 2000.

claim: HSP90 is essential for ERα dimer formation.
source: HSP90 is essential for ERα hormone binding (Fliss et al., 2000), dimer formation (Powell et al., 2010), and binding to the EREs (Inano et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Powell et al., 2010.

claim: HSP90 is essential for ERα binding to the EREs.
source: HSP90 is essential for ERα hormone binding (Fliss et al., 2000), dimer formation (Powell et al., 2010), and binding to the EREs (Inano et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Inano et al., 1994.

claim: The passage of the ER to the cell membrane requires association with the HSP27 (HSPB1) oligomers in the cytoplasm.
source: Also, the passage of the ER to the cell membrane requires association with the HSP27 (HSPB1) oligomers in the cytoplasm (Razandi et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Razandi et al., 2010.

claim: More than 20 chaperones and co-chaperones associated with ERα in human cells have been identified through a quantitative proteomic approach.
source: More than 20 chaperones and co-chaperones associated with ERα in human cells have been identified through a quantitative proteomic approach (Dhamad et al., 2016), but their specific contribution in the receptor action still needs to be investigated.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Dhamad et al., 2016.

claim: HSF1 is involved in the regulation of a plethora of non-HSP genes, which support oncogenic processes: cell cycle regulation, signaling, metabolism, adhesion, and translation.
source: Moreover, HSF1 is involved in the regulation of a plethora of non-HSP genes, which support oncogenic processes: cell cycle regulation, signaling, metabolism, adhesion, and translation (Mendillo et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mendillo et al., 2012.

claim: A high level of HSF1 expression was found in cancer cell lines and many human tumors.
source: A high level of HSF1 expression was found in cancer cell lines and many human tumors (Vydra et al., 2014; De Thonel et al., 2011) and was shown to be associated with the increased mortality of ER-positive breast cancer patients (Santagata et al., 2011; Gökmen-Polar and Badve, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Vydra et al., 2014 and De Thonel et al., 2011.

claim: High level of HSF1 expression was shown to be associated with the increased mortality of ER-positive breast cancer patients.
source: A high level of HSF1 expression was found in cancer cell lines and many human tumors (Vydra et al., 2014; De Thonel et al., 2011) and was shown to be associated with the increased mortality of ER-positive breast cancer patients (Santagata et al., 2011; Gökmen-Polar and Badve, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Santagata et al., 2011 and Gökmen-Polar and Badve, 2016.

claim: E2-activated HSF1 is transcriptionally potent and takes part in the regulation of several genes essential for breast cancer cell growth.
source: E2-activated HSF1 is transcriptionally potent and takes part in the regulation of several genes essential for breast cancer cell growth (Vydra et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Vydra et al., 2019, which is the authors' previous work.

claim: HSF1 knockdown reduced HSF1 level about 10-fold in MCF7 cells.
source: Then, the most potent variant that reduced HSF1 level about 10-fold (termed afterward shHSF1) was chosen for further studies.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from western blot analyses (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).

claim: The heat shock response was significantly reduced in HSF1 knockdown MCF7 cells.
source: Although the heat shock response was significantly reduced, the expression of HSP genes (HSPA1A, HSPH1, HSPB1, and HSPB8) was still induced after this HSF1 knockdown (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from RT-qPCR analyses (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).

claim: The expression of HSP genes (HSPA1A, HSPH1, HSPB1, and HSPB8) was still induced after HSF1 knockdown in MCF7 cells.
source: Although the heat shock response was significantly reduced, the expression of HSP genes (HSPA1A, HSPH1, HSPB1, and HSPB8) was still induced after this HSF1 knockdown (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from RT-qPCR analyses (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).

claim: Complete elimination of HSF1 was connected with a substantial loss of inducibility of HSP genes following hyperthermia in MCF7 cells.
source: The complete elimination of HSF1 (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) was connected with a substantial loss of inducibility of HSP genes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) and proteins (HSP105/HSPH1, HSP90, HSP70/HSPA1) following hyperthermia (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from RT-qPCR and western blot analyses (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).

claim: The ability of MCF7 cells to form colonies in the clonogenic assay was reduced in all experimental models of HSF1 depletion.
source: The ability of cells to form colonies in the clonogenic assay was reduced in all MCF7 experimental models of HSF1 depletion (using shRNA and sgRNA; Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from clonogenic assays (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).

claim: The population size of ALDH-positive (stem/progenitor) cells correlated with the HSF1 level and was reduced in HSF1-deficient MCF7 cells.
source: Moreover, the population size of ALDH-positive (stem/progenitor) cells correlated with the HSF1 level and was reduced in HSF1-deficient cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ALDEFLUOR assays (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).

claim: The increased contribution of cells in the G1 phase was associated with the HSF1 knockout in MCF7 cells.
source: Also, the increased contribution of cells in the G1 phase was associated with the HSF1 knockout (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from cell cycle analyses (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).

claim: HSF1 knockdown did not affect the proliferation rate of MCF7 cells.
source: HSF1 knockdown did not affect the proliferation rate, while the functional HSF1 knockout led to a slight reduction in the proliferation rate under standard conditions (this effect was not visible under less favorable growing conditions, i.e., in phenol red-free 5% dextran-activated charcoal-stripped fetal bovine serum (FBS); Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from proliferation assays (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).

claim: The functional HSF1 knockout led to a slight reduction in the proliferation rate of MCF7 cells under standard conditions.
source: HSF1 knockdown did not affect the proliferation rate, while the functional HSF1 knockout led to a slight reduction in the proliferation rate under standard conditions (this effect was not visible under less favorable growing conditions, i.e., in phenol red-free 5% dextran-activated charcoal-stripped fetal bovine serum (FBS); Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from proliferation assays (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).

claim: HSF1− T47D cells grew slightly faster than HSF1+ cells under standard conditions.
source: Unlike MCF7 cells, HSF1− T47D cells grew slightly faster than HSF1+ cells, but this difference was not statistically significant and no differences were observed in the cell cycle (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from proliferation assays (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).

claim: Stimulation of HSF1-proficient MCF7 cells with E2 for 7–14 days resulted in cell-cell dissociation and the acquisition of an ameboid- or mesenchymal-like morphology.
source: We noticed that stimulation of HSF1-proficient MCF7 cells with E2 for 7–14 days resulted in cell-cell dissociation, the acquisition of an ameboid- or mesenchymal-like morphology (Figure 1E and F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1I), and enhanced adhesion to collagens (I and IV) but reduced to vitronectin (Figure 1G; adhesion to fibronectin, laminin, and tenascin was not affected; not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from F-actin staining (Figure 1E and F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1I).

claim: Stimulation of HSF1-proficient MCF7 cells with E2 for 7–14 days resulted in enhanced adhesion to collagens (I and IV).
source: We noticed that stimulation of HSF1-proficient MCF7 cells with E2 for 7–14 days resulted in cell-cell dissociation, the acquisition of an ameboid- or mesenchymal-like morphology (Figure 1E and F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1I), and enhanced adhesion to collagens (I and IV) but reduced to vitronectin (Figure 1G; adhesion to fibronectin, laminin, and tenascin was not affected; not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from cell adhesion assays (Figure 1G).

claim: Stimulation of HSF1-proficient MCF7 cells with E2 for 7–14 days resulted in reduced adhesion to vitronectin.
source: We noticed that stimulation of HSF1-proficient MCF7 cells with E2 for 7–14 days resulted in cell-cell dissociation, the acquisition of an ameboid- or mesenchymal-like morphology (Figure 1E and F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1I), and enhanced adhesion to collagens (I and IV) but reduced to vitronectin (Figure 1G; adhesion to fibronectin, laminin, and tenascin was not affected; not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from cell adhesion assays (Figure 1G).

claim: E2 treatment did not affect adhesion to fibronectin, laminin, and tenascin in HSF1-proficient MCF7 cells.
source: We noticed that stimulation of HSF1-proficient MCF7 cells with E2 for 7–14 days resulted in cell-cell dissociation, the acquisition of an ameboid- or mesenchymal-like morphology (Figure 1E and F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1I), and enhanced adhesion to collagens (I and IV) but reduced to vitronectin (Figure 1G; adhesion to fibronectin, laminin, and tenascin was not affected; not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from cell adhesion assays (not shown in figures).

claim: E2 treatment enabled HSF1-proficient MCF7 cells to migrate faster.
source: These changes enabled cells to migrate faster (Figure 1H, Figure 1—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Boyden chamber assays (Figure 1H, Figure 1—figure supplement 1H).

claim: Amoeboid-like morphology was dominant among the scattered MCF7 cells after E2 treatment.
source: Amoeboid-like morphology was dominant among the scattered MCF7 cells, while mesenchymal-like morphology was dominant in T47D cells (Figure 1E and F, Figure 1—figure supplement 2D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from F-actin staining (Figure 1E and F).

claim: Mesenchymal-like morphology was dominant in T47D cells after E2 treatment.
source: Amoeboid-like morphology was dominant among the scattered MCF7 cells, while mesenchymal-like morphology was dominant in T47D cells (Figure 1E and F, Figure 1—figure supplement 2D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from F-actin staining (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D and E).

claim: Adhesion to collagens was not affected by E2 in T47D cells.
source: Also, adhesion to collagens was not affected by E2 in T47D cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from cell adhesion assays (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F).

claim: E2 treatment enhanced migration of HSF1-proficient but not HSF1-deficient T47D cells.
source: Nevertheless, E2 treatment enhanced migration of HSF1-proficient but not HSF1-deficient T47D cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Boyden chamber assays (Figure 1—figure supplement 2G).

claim: 50 genes were similarly regulated by E2 (47 upregulated and 3 downregulated) in all HSF1-proficient MCF7 cell variants.
source: We found 50 genes similarly regulated by E2 (47 upregulated and 3 downregulated) in all HSF1-proficient MCF7 cell variants (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B).

claim: Only 13 genes were similarly upregulated after E2 stimulation in HSF1-deficient MCF7 cell variants.
source: On the other hand, only 13 genes were similarly upregulated after E2 stimulation in HSF1-deficient MCF7 cell variants (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and C).

claim: HSF1 deficiency negatively affected the processes activated by estrogen (the early and late estrogen response).
source: The gene set enrichment analyses indicated that HSF1 deficiency negatively affected the processes activated by estrogen (the early and late estrogen response; Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene set enrichment analyses (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).

claim: Almost all genes upregulated by E2 in HSF1-proficient cells were also upregulated in HSF1-deficient cells (except NAPRT).
source: Moreover, though almost all genes upregulated by E2 in HSF1-proficient cells were also upregulated in HSF1-deficient cells (except NAPRT), the degree of their activation (measured as a fold change E2 versus Ctr) was usually weaker in the latter cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F), which indicated that the transcriptional response to estrogen was inhibited in the lack of HSF1.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).

claim: Several E2-dependent genes revealed slightly higher basal expression (without E2 stimulation) in HSF1-deficient cells.
source: Interestingly, however, several E2-dependent genes revealed slightly higher basal expression (without E2 stimulation) in HSF1-deficient cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G), which suggested that in the absence of E2, HSF1 could be involved in the suppression of these genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G).

claim: In the absence of E2, HSF1 could be involved in the suppression of E2-dependent genes.
source: Interestingly, however, several E2-dependent genes revealed slightly higher basal expression (without E2 stimulation) in HSF1-deficient cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G), which suggested that in the absence of E2, HSF1 could be involved in the suppression of these genes.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that E2-dependent genes have higher basal expression in HSF1-deficient cells.

claim: 3715 genes significantly changed the expression (2336 upregulated and 1479 downregulated) in HSF1+ MCF7 cells after E2 stimulation.
source: The analysis showed that 3715 genes significantly changed the expression (2336 upregulated and 1479 downregulated) in HSF1+ cells after E2 stimulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data (Figure 2A).

claim: Only 2969 genes (1818 upregulated and 1151 downregulated) changed the expression in HSF1− MCF7 cells after E2 stimulation.
source: On the other hand, only 2969 genes (1818 upregulated and 1151 downregulated) changed the expression in HSF1− cells (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data (Figure 2A).

claim: Approximately 20% of genes responding to E2 treatment in HSF1+ cells did not respond similarly in HSF1− cells.
source: Thus, approximately 20% of genes responding to E2 treatment in HSF1+ cells did not respond similarly in HSF1− cells.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the RNA-seq data showing differences in the number of E2-responsive genes between HSF1+ and HSF1− cells (Figure 2A).

claim: Among genes up- or downregulated in both HSF1+ and HSF1− MCF7 cell variants, approximately 68% or 81%, respectively, responded less effectively (fold change E2 versus Ctr) in HSF1− cells than HSF1+ cells.
source: Moreover, among genes up- or downregulated in both cell variants, approximately 68% or 81%, respectively, responded less effectively (fold change E2 versus Ctr) in HSF1− cells than HSF1+ cells (Figure 2A, bottom panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data (Figure 2A, bottom panel).

claim: Gene set enrichment analyses revealed slight differences in the early and late estrogen response pathways between HSF1+ and HSF1− MCF7 cells.
source: The gene set enrichment analyses revealed the slight differences in the early and late estrogen response pathways (Hallmark gene sets M5906 and M5907) but also in genes defining epithelial-mesenchymal transition (M5930).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene set enrichment analyses (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).

claim: The expression of genes from early and late estrogen response pathways already differentiated untreated HSF1− and HSF1+ MCF7 cells.
source: Interestingly, the expression of genes from these pathways already differentiated untreated HSF1− and HSF1+ cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by gene set enrichment analyses (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).

claim: Genes encoding cell cycle-related targets of E2F transcription factors (M5925), involved in the G2/M checkpoint (M5901) as well as ECM proteoglycans (M27219) and collagen formation (M631), discriminated HSF1− and HSF1+ MCF7 cells.
source: Genes encoding cell cycle-related targets of E2F transcription factors (M5925), involved in the G2/M checkpoint (M5901) as well as ECM proteoglycans (M27219) and collagen formation (M631), also discriminated HSF1− and HSF1+ cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene set enrichment analyses (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).

claim: Signaling pathways related to proliferation, migration, and collagen adhesion were identified as primarily affected by HSF1 deficiency.
source: In addition, signaling pathways related to proliferation, migration, and collagen adhesion were identified as primarily affected, which was consistent with the results of functional tests.
evidence: This claim is supported by gene set enrichment analyses (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A) and is consistent with functional test results.

claim: 46 genes were upregulated and 2 were downregulated after E2 treatment in all MCF7 cell models.
source: Among E2-responding genes that were common for all MCF7 cell models, 46 were upregulated and 2 were downregulated (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data (Figure 2B).

claim: In unstimulated cells ERα binding was more efficient (more binding sites and increased number of tags per peak) in HSF1-deficient cell variant (KO#2) than in the corresponding HSF1-proficient control (MIX cells).
source: These analyses revealed that in unstimulated cells ERα binding was more efficient (more binding sites and increased number of tags per peak) in HSF1-deficient cell variant (KO#2) than in the corresponding HSF1-proficient control (MIX cells) (Figure 3A and B) (it is worth noting that the MIX cell variant was also different from wild-type cells, indicating that the genome organization was affected by the CRISPR/Cas9 procedure itself, possibly due to off-targets).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq data (Figure 3A and B).

claim: Estrogen treatment for 30 or 60 min resulted in enhanced ERα binding in all MCF7 cell variants.
source: Estrogen treatment for 30 or 60 min resulted in enhanced ERα binding in all cell variants.
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq data (Figure 3A, Figure 3C).

claim: Fold enrichment (E2 versus Ctr) of ERα binding was lower in HSF1-deficient cells than in HSF1-proficient cells.
source: However, fold enrichment (E2 versus Ctr) was lower in HSF1-deficient cells than in HSF1-proficient cells (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq data (Figure 3C).

claim: The number of detected ERα peaks in the E2-treated HSF1-deficient cells was only slightly higher than in unstimulated cells.
source: Moreover, the number of detected peaks in the E2-treated HSF1-deficient cells was only slightly higher than in unstimulated cells (Figure 3A) and enhanced ERα binding was primarily manifested in sites already existing in unstimulated cells (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq data (Figure 3A).

claim: Enhanced ERα binding after E2 treatment was primarily manifested in sites already existing in unstimulated HSF1-deficient cells.
source: Moreover, the number of detected peaks in the E2-treated HSF1-deficient cells was only slightly higher than in unstimulated cells (Figure 3A) and enhanced ERα binding was primarily manifested in sites already existing in unstimulated cells (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq data (Figure 3C and D).

claim: After estrogen treatment, ERβ (ESR2) and ERα (ESR1) motifs were centrally enriched in ERα-binding regions in all MCF7 cell variants.

evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that HSF1 influences the formation of ERα-mediated chromatin loops, and is illustrated in Figure 9.

source: Moreover, HSF1 may be involved in the repression of unliganded ERα.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that HSF1 deficiency results in enhanced binding of unliganded ERα and higher basal expression of ERα-regulated genes.

claim: Genes activated by ERα and HSF1 play an important role in regulating the growth and spread of estrogen-dependent tumors.
